title: Infinite Series
body:
[[Taylor Series]]
[[Maclaurin Series]]

---

An infinite sum, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n = a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \cdots$. You cannot add infinitely
many things, so the sum is **defined** as the [[Limit]] of what you can add:

$$
s_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n
\qquad\qquad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n = \lim_{N\to\infty}s_N
$$

$s_N$ is the $N$th **partial sum**, and the sequence $\{s_N\}$ is the real object of study. If it
converges the series converges and its value is that limit; if not, the series diverges and **the
symbol $\sum a_n$ does not name a number at all**. A divergent series has no value to manipulate,
which is why rearranging one produces nonsense.

The claim worth pausing on: an infinite sum of positive numbers can be finite. $\frac12 + \frac14 +
\frac18 + \cdots = 1$. Once that is believable, a function can be an infinite polynomial, and that
is [[Power Series]] and [[Taylor Series]], which is where the course is going.

## The terms going to zero is not enough

$$
\sum a_n \text{ converges} \Rightarrow a_n \to 0
\qquad\qquad
a_n \to 0 \not\Rightarrow \sum a_n \text{ converges}
$$

**The harmonic series is the counterexample the whole block hangs on.** $\sum \frac1n$ has terms
going to zero and diverges, by grouping:

```
1 + 1/2 + (1/3+1/4) + (1/5+…+1/8) + (1/9+…+1/16) + …
      1/2  >  1/2      >  1/2         >  1/2
```

Each bracket exceeds $\frac12$ and there are infinitely many brackets. The partial sums grow like
$\ln N$: slowly, forever. Read the contrapositive of the first implication and you have the $n$th
term test, which is **only a divergence test**. See [[Convergence Tests]].

## The two families to know cold

**Geometric.** $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}ar^n$ converges **iff $|r| < 1$**, and then

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}ar^n = \frac{a}{1-r}
$$

The only common series whose **sum** you can write down rather than merely test. Derived by the
telescoping trick $s_N - rs_N = a - ar^N$, and it is the source of $0.\overline{9} = 1$, of the
$\frac{1}{1-x}$ [[Maclaurin Series]], and of $\sum_{i=0}^{k}\frac{n}{2^i} < 2n$, the bound that
makes halving algorithms linear rather than $n\log n$ in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]].

**$p$-series.** $\sum \frac{1}{n^p}$ converges **iff $p > 1$**. Same threshold as
$\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx$ in [[Improper Integral]], and the integral test is the reason. $p = 1$ is
the harmonic series, sitting exactly on the boundary and failing.

**Telescoping** is the third one that can actually be summed: if
$a_n = b_n - b_{n+1}$, everything cancels and $s_N = b_1 - b_{N+1}$.
[[Integration By Partial Fractions]] is how you find the $b_n$, since
$\frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac1n - \frac{1}{n+1}$ is that decomposition.

## Absolute and conditional convergence

$\sum a_n$ **converges absolutely** if $\sum|a_n|$ converges. Absolute convergence implies
convergence; the reverse fails. A series that converges while $\sum|a_n|$ diverges converges
**conditionally**, and $\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} = \ln 2$ is the example.

The distinction is not pedantry. **A conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to sum to
any number you choose**, or to diverge (Riemann's rearrangement theorem). An absolutely convergent
one cannot: it behaves like a finite sum. So "does the order of addition matter" has an answer, and
it is this.
